notes.meaning: God reminds Jerusalem that she completely forgot where she came from. Long ago, she was like an abandoned newborn baby left in an open field to die in her own blood until God took pity on her and gave her life. Forgetting His past grace led the people into pride, ingratitude, and shameful idolatry.

God cries out in grief and warning over Jerusalem's terrible guilt. Not content with their past sins, the people built public shrines and pagan altars in every street and open square. They turned the holy city into a wide-open brothel for false worship that could be seen by everyone.

Jerusalem set up idol altars at every busy crossroad so no traveler could miss them. God had made the nation lovely and famous, but she degraded that beauty by chasing after every passing false god. Instead of waiting to be courted, she aggressively offered herself to any foreign idol.

God's people sought political alliances with Egypt and adopted their crude and corrupt pagan religion. Israel forgot how the Lord had rescued them from Egyptian slavery and eagerly took up those old practices again. This willful disloyalty directly provoked the Lord to anger.

God struck the nation with discipline by cutting back their food, wealth, and territory. He also let their enemies, the Philistines, conquer and plunder them. Even the pagan Philistines were shocked by how easily Israel threw away her own God, yet this painful correction still did not make Jerusalem repent.

Jerusalem was still not satisfied with her Egyptian and local idols, so she sought out the distant Assyrians. King Ahaz and the people paid for Assyrian military help and brought Assyrian altars right into the temple worship. Their restless craving for foreign alliances and new gods could never be filled.

The people expanded their unfaithfulness all the way to Babylon, the great trading empire of the Chaldeans. They copied the corrupt practices of ancient Canaan and combined them with the dark superstitions of Babylon. Even after welcoming every idol from the known world, their desire remained completely unsatisfied.

The Lord declares that Jerusalem's heart was completely weak and lacking all self-control. Sin had made the people morally powerless to resist temptation, like water poured out on the ground. At the same time, they were headstrong and arrogant, refusing to be guided or corrected by God.

Jerusalem built high places in every street, but she acted worse than an ordinary prostitute. A common prostitute sells herself because she needs money or food, but Jerusalem scorned payment and gave herself away for nothing. She ran after sin purely for the sake of rebelling against the Lord.

Jerusalem was like a married woman who had everything provided by her husband yet betrayed him with strangers. God had entered into a holy marriage covenant with Israel, loving and protecting her. Her sin was far worse than regular prostitution because it was a direct betrayal of her faithful Husband.

Normal prostitutes are paid by their lovers, but Jerusalem did the exact opposite by paying foreign nations to come to her. Kings of Judah took silver and gold from the royal palace and the temple to buy the friendship of Assyria and Egypt. No nation had chased after Israel; she spent God's treasures to entice foreign nations to corrupt her.

God addresses Jerusalem by the shameful title she had earned for herself and tells her to listen to His word. The message now shifts from listing her crimes to announcing her formal legal sentence. God is about to act as a righteous judge against His unfaithful covenant people.

The Lord lists the charges that bring about Jerusalem's judgment. She squandered her wealth on pagan treaties, publicly exposed her shame in idol worship, and sacrificed her own children in fire to false gods like Molech. The holy city had become guilty of both spiritual unfaithfulness and terrible bloodshed.

God promises to summon all the surrounding nations against Jerusalem. Both the foreign partners she courted, such as Egypt and Babylon, and her bitter enemies, such as Edom and Philistia, would surround her. God would strip away all her defenses and leave her fully exposed and disgraced before their eyes.

Under the law of Moses, both adulterers and murderers were sentenced to death. Because Jerusalem broke her marriage vows to God and slaughtered her own children, she deserved both death sentences. God would bring upon her the full fury of His righteous jealousy and anger for shedding innocent blood.

The Lord would hand Jerusalem over to the very pagan nations she had tried to win over. Those invaders would smash down her idol shrines, steal her royal jewelry, and strip the city down to bare stone. Just as she was once an abandoned infant with nothing, she would be left completely bare once more.

The invading Babylonian army would act like a legal mob carrying out capital punishment on an adulterous city. They would stone Jerusalem with heavy rocks flung from catapults and battering engines, and cut down the fleeing people with the sword. These weapons fulfilled the ancient penalties of the law on an apostate city.

The Babylonian invaders would burn down the houses, the palaces, and the temple of Jerusalem while neighboring nations looked on. This harsh public judgment would bring a total end to the people's idolatry and political scheming. After the exile, the Jewish people would never again fall into the worship of physical idols.

God's fierce anger and jealousy would finally quiet down after the full penalty was paid. The judgment would be so complete that there would be nothing left to punish. Once divine justice was satisfied and the sin was wiped away, the storm of God's wrath would come to an end.

differ.view: God's anger rests not out of pity, but because His justice has fully consumed the wicked city until nothing remains to destroy.
God's fury ceases because the people's idolatry truly came to an end through the exile, removing the cause of His contention with them.
God becoming calm means He completely abandons the unfaithful nation to her ruin, ceasing even to warn or correct her.
